figures.caption: Typical cross-section of a soil nail wall. Modified after Porterfield et al. (1994)
figures.description: Introduction Overview of soil nail wall construction and where it fits. Top-down construction: excavate a lift, install nails and initial shotcrete facing, repeat; then final facing Nail vertical spacing most often 4 to 6 ft; horizontal spacing often 4 to 6 ft Stable excavation lift commonly 3 to 5 ft high, more in some soils Nails transfer load to the soil behind; facing supports soil between nails and makes the wall act as a unit Suited to ground that can stand in short vertical or sub-vertical unsupported cuts Mostly permanent in U.S. roadway projects; also temporary shoring (a few months) Elements of a Soil Nail Wall Components of a soil nail wall; see the subsections. Soil Nails Components of the soil nail itself. Tendon tension mobilizes with lateral movement of the retained soil

figures.caption: Illustration. Typical soil nail wall construction sequence. Modified after Porterfield et al. (1994)
figures.description: Construction Sequence Step-by-step construction of a soil nail wall. Initial lift 2.5 to 7 ft, typically 3 to 5 ft, slightly below the first nail row Face must stand unsupported until nails and facing are in, typically one to two days Grout placed by tremie under gravity or low pressure (less than 5 to 10 psi); hollow bars drill and grout in one operation Strip drains placed between nails and unrolled down to the next lift Initial facing typically lightly reinforced 4-in. shotcrete, WWM at mid-thickness Bearing plate pressed into fresh shotcrete; hex nut wrench-tightened within 24 hours Minimum 3-day shotcrete strength before the next lift; 72 hours for planning WWM panels overlap at least one full mesh cell Final facing: CIP concrete, reinforced shotcrete or prefabricated panels;

figures.caption: Illustration. Hybrid soil nail/MSE wall. Source: Wood et al. (2009)
figures.description: Hybrid Soil Nail Walls Combining soil nails with MSE walls or ground anchors. MSE plus soil nail walls may be more economical in cut/fill than full-height MSE or drilled shaft walls (Wood et al. 2009) Utilities in the upper zone: facing cantilevers 8 to 10 ft with one or two ground anchor rows, nails below Soil nails not generally suited to deep-seated slip surfaces; add ground anchors Tiered walls: nails at the top of the slope, long anchors through the slip plane for global stability

figures.caption: Illustration. SMSE wall for steep terrain. Modified after Morrison et al. (2006)
figures.description: Shored Mechanically Stabilized Earth (SMSE) Walls Shored MSE walls for road widening in steep terrain. figures.description: Tendons Selecting soil nail tendon grade, size and length. Threaded bars: continuous thread or cut threads (account for reduced area); at least 6 in. of thread on the cut face Grade 60 or 75 (60 or 75 ksi) per ASTM A615 generally used Grade 95 acceptable if ductility comparable to lower grades; Grade 150 per ASTM A722, more typical of ground anchors Common sizes Nos. 8, 9, 10, 11; Nos. 6-7 often avoided; No. 14 and larger may be inefficient Maximum manufactured length 60 ft for Nos. 6-14; couplers must develop the bar's nominal tensile resistance Hollow bars: yield 60-90 ksi, OD about 1-3 in., wall 0.3-1 in., 10- and 20-ft lengths Section properties: Table A.1 (solid), Tables A.2-A.4 (hollow), Appendix A

figures.description: Connection Components Nail head connection hardware. Plate, nut and washers connect to the initial facing; headed studs connect to the final facing Bearing plate: Grade 36 (AASHTO M183/ASTM A36) or Grade 50; square, 8-10 in. sides, 0.75-1 in. thick Plate well seated in fresh shotcrete but not excessively embedded Beveled washers or spherical seat nuts for uniform bearing Nuts hand-wrench tightened; avoid over-tightening after shotcrete sets; AASHTO M291/ASTM A563 Grade B Typically four headed studs welded to the plate (ANSI/AWS 2000), commonly 1-1.5 in. from plate edges

figures.description: Excavation Excavation and temporary face stability during soil nail construction. Install surface water controls and collector trenches before excavating Initial cut often 3 to 5 ft; smooth face; hand excavation for cobbles and boulders Working bench ~30 ft wide; small track drills: 15 ft bench, 8-10 ft headroom Lowest safety margin often while a lower lift is unsupported Signs of instability (bulging, sloughing, deformation): backfill with a temporary berm at once Expose only what can be shotcreted in one shift Stabilizing berm: nails through the berm, or slots no wider than about the nail horizontal spacing Alternatives: soldier piles and anchors, permeation grouting (LaRue 2010), vertical grouted bars at 1-3 ft

figures.description: Requirements for Selecting Location and Number of Exploratory Borings Laying out borings for a soil nail wall. Borings along the centerline, in front of and behind the wall (Figure 4.1; AASHTO 2012 Table 10.4.2-1) Centerline: spacing 100-200 ft; depth at least H below the excavation bottom Behind: spacing up to 150 ft; H to 1.5H behind the wall; depth at least 2H below final grade Upward slope behind: borings 1.5H to 2H from the wall, deep enough for larger sliding masses In front: spacing up to 200 ft; 0.75H to H in front; depth at least H below the excavation bottom Soft soils, organic silt or peat: deepen by H (behind and along) or 0.5H (in front) Seismic areas: to the base of liquefiable deposits within about 2H Maximum depth generally need not exceed about 50 ft Weathered rock: core

figures.caption: Illustration. Potential slip surfaces and soil nail tensile forces
figures.description: Load Transfer Mechanisms How load develops in soil nails during staged construction. First lift height chosen so the cut stands unsupported before nailing Soil deformation loads the facing; load passes to the nails and by grout-soil shear to the soil Nail force rises from the facing to Tmax near the critical slip surface, then falls toward the nail end Deeper lifts move the slip surface and Tmax back and load lower nails more; upper nails may unload Upper nails stay important for local stability Post-construction nail force increase up to about 15% (creep, stress relaxation); allow for it in bond strength Check intermediate and final stages, including an unsupported lift before nailing, worse with seepage

figures.caption: Illustration. Drainage of soil nail walls
figures.description: Long-Term Surface Water and Groundwater Control Permanent drainage of soil nail walls under low and high groundwater. Strip drain spacing 1.0 SH to 2.0 SH, SH most common Weepholes: 2- to 4-in. PVC, 12 to 16 in. long, 8 to 10 ft apart along the base, with at least 1 ft3 filter plug Underdrain alternative: Schedule 40 PVC toe drain in clean aggregate wrapped in geotextile (not geotextile on the pipe) High groundwater: seepage analysis; keep water at least 2 ft below the nails and the facing base Drain pipes: 2-in. slotted or perforated PVC at 5 to 10 degrees upslope, 1 to 3 ft or longer, about one per 100 ft2 of face Drain pipes need long-term maintenance; clogging reduces stability Permanent interception ditch behind the wall

figures.description: Stepped Walls Design of stepped (benched) soil nail walls. Stepped walls need shorter nails than non-stepped walls of the same height; less frequent on transportation projects Setback < about 1/20 of combined height acts as a battered wall (about 3 degrees) Setback > lower wall height H2: walls independent; otherwise analyze the lower wall with the upper one Upper MSE wall as surcharge and shear (conservative) or both walls in a general slope stability program Bench sloped and lined to avoid ponding and infiltration

figures.caption: Illustration. Composite wall structures: (a) cross section, and (b) soil nail walls with concrete piles. Source: Byrne et al. (1988)
figures.description: Composite Walls Soil nail walls combined with ground anchors or MSE walls. Composite walls are typically soil nails with ground anchors, installed top-down (Figure 6.15) Anchors cannot usually be tensioned against initial shotcrete without bearing pads or a thicker facing Consider the anchors' vertical component, especially above 20 degrees Anchors for global instability: preferably near the bottom, tensioned after the final facing Analyze nails for slip surfaces within 1.5 nail lengths behind the top; anchors for deeper ones (GEC No. 4, Sabatini et al. 1999)

figures.caption: Illustration. Strut-nail concept. Source: Byrne et al. (1998)
figures.description: Strut-Nails Design and applications of strut-nails (toe-nails). Strut-nails: steep (about 15-20 to 45 degrees from vertical), short, in compression, vertical support of the facing Designed like Case I micropiles (Sabatini et al. 2005) by equilibrium of W, CST and TT TT is added to the axial load of the nail above Opposing horizontal components add facing bending; install close to or staggered within the bottom row Check buckling as for micropiles; a stub casing increases resistance Typical use: final facing support where the wall ends at bedrock; vertical elements at about 2 to 3 ft in poor soils

figures.caption: Illustration. Examples of frost protection: (a) first example, and (b) second example. Modified after Byrne et al. (1998)
figures.description: Considerations for Frost Protection Frost protection of soil nail walls. Soil nail walls are always susceptible to frost because of the exposed facing Porous backfill, facing slightly thicker than the frost depth, larger tendons, insulation 1 in. of EPS foam considered thermally equivalent to 1 ft of gravel; select by R-value North-facing walls may have 1.4 to 2 times the frost penetration of south-facing walls

figures.caption: Illustration. Typical comprehensive monitoring instrumentation. Source: Byrne et al. (1998)
figures.description: Monitoring and Action Plan Monitoring and action plans for soil nail walls. Minimum: face movement by survey markers and inclinometers 3 to 8 ft behind the facing (not beyond 30 percent of H for one row) Minimum: top-of-wall and ground movement, ground cracks (daily), facing deterioration, drainage Over fine-grained soils, watch the toe for cracking or bulging (basal heave, global instability) Comprehensive: paired strain gauges at 5-ft spacing; inclinometer arrays (Figure 9.7) Design documents define instruments, frequencies, reporting and parties Movement thresholds and an action plan (typically by the Contractor) are essential

figures.caption: Photo. Strain gauge attached to a sister bar. Photograph courtesy of Schnabel Engineering
figures.description: Monitoring Instruments Instruments for monitoring soil nail walls. Select instruments by parameter, reliability, simplicity and readout compatibility Inclinometers most comprehensive; in-place types checked with a manual probe periodically Survey prisms by optical or EDM methods: 0.1 in. or better within 300 ft Automated total stations reduce reading errors and separate environmental from gravity movements Vibrating wire strain gauges with sister bars (Figure 9.8) most common in the U.S.; strain = microstrain x 10^-6 Nail head load cells occasionally read inaccurately
